Let's consider the structure of maximal triangle-free graphs.
A well-known class of maximal triangle-free graphs are complete bipartite graphs $K_{n, m}$ where $n+m = |V|$.
In a complete bipartite graph, vertices are partitioned into sets $A$ and $B$. All edges between $A$ and $B$ exist. No edges within $A$ or within $B$.
Is it triangle-free? Yes, any cycle must alternate between $A$ and $B$, so length is even. No triangles.
Is it maximal?
If we add an edge within $A$, say between $u, v \in A$, then pick any $w \in B$. Since it's complete bipartite, $u \sim w$ and $v \sim w$. So $u, v, w$ form a triangle.
So yes, complete bipartite graphs are maximal triangle-free.
